CausalChain: Hepatic PPARβ/δ activation -> increased production of PC (18:0/18:1) -> secretion of PC (18:0/18:1) into circulation -> activation of muscle PPARα -> enhanced fatty acid oxidation in muscle -> maintenance of systemic lipid homeostasis; In NAFLD: elevated hepatic PPARγ activation -> suppression of PPARβ/δ-driven PC (18:0/18:1) synthesis -> reduced circulating PC (18:0/18:1) levels -> diminished muscle PPARα activation -> decreased muscle fatty acid oxidation -> exacerbated systemic lipid accumulation and hepatic steatosis.
Hypothesis: Hepatic overactivation of PPARγ in NAFLD disrupts the PPARβ/δ‐mediated production of PC (18:0/18:1), leading to reduced activation of muscle PPARα and impaired peripheral fatty acid oxidation, thereby contributing to systemic dyslipidemia and progression of liver disease.
Abstract: Recent advances in understanding the distinct roles of hepatic peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptors (PPARs) suggest that inter-pathway communication may critically determine whole-body lipid homeostasis. Here, we propose a novel hypothesis in which excessive activation of hepatic PPARγ, a hallmark of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), disrupts a previously unrecognized metabolic circuit mediated by hepatic PPARβ/δ. Under normal conditions, hepatic PPARβ/δ drives the synthesis of phosphatidylcholine (PC) (18:0/18:1), a lipid mediator that, upon secretion, activates PPARα in skeletal muscle to promote fatty acid oxidation and energy expenditure. We hypothesize that in the NAFLD liver, heightened PPARγ activity suppresses the PPARβ/δ–PC (18:0/18:1) pathway. This suppression leads to reduced muscle PPARα activation, thereby impairing peripheral lipid utilization and exacerbating systemic dyslipidemia. This crosstalk disruption may contribute to the progression of hepatic steatosis and systemic insulin resistance, providing a novel target for therapeutic intervention.
